Parent: yes. Two policy tests passed; the brace test exposed that the escaped-format case wasn’t producing the expected issue. I’m isolating that path now with a decoder unit test and a direct escaped literal, then I’ll rerun the policy suite and record the fix.

The escape bug is in the shared decoder: Python’s tree-sitter nests escape nodes under `string_content`, while the decoder previously copied that parent text unchanged. I’ve updated it to decode those structured child nodes, preserving raw-string behavior and source mappings; the focused decoder test is queued now.

The decoder change is ready; the Python unit test is still waiting for one of the three shared build slots. Once it runs, I’ll rerun the full Python unit suite and the policy fixtures against the corrected escape decoding.

The decoder regression and all 59 Python crate unit tests pass, including raw and adjacent-string behavior. The corrected policy rerun is still waiting behind other lanes’ build jobs; once it completes, I’ll proceed with clippy and the required vocabulary checks.

The policy rerun has the build slot and is recompiling the facade with the corrected Python decoder. No test results are available yet; the prior percent and incomplete-boundary tests already passed, and the brace test is the remaining check for the fix.

The rerun has reached the flow layer after recompiling Python, RQL, and analysis dependencies. Other lanes and CI are using the remaining slots, but this build is progressing; I’m letting the configured queue manage concurrency and will continue as soon as the test result is ready.

The policy rerun has moved through policy, runtime, and MCP dependencies and is nearing the test binary. The string decoder’s full crate suite is green, so this run will confirm the fix through the actual RQL policy path.

The decoded escape case now passes. The same brace fixture found a separate overlap: `{name}.format("one")` is selected as both missing-named and surplus-positional under the current rule logic. I’m checking the rule’s positional-field boundary so the fixture and result reflect the intended behavior precisely.

The reference query confirms the boundary: surplus positional arguments are counted against positional format fields, and named-only formats have no positional field count. I’ve gated surplus detection on at least one positional field, keeping the named-only call in the missing-named rule without a false surplus finding.

The rule-boundary fix is in, and the updated policy run is waiting for a shared build slot again. The previous run’s two other policy tests remain green; this rerun rebuilds the RQL crate with the positional-field guard before checking all three fixtures.

The decoded-literal case is now handled. The remaining brace-policy mismatch is still the surplus-argument rule, so I’m tracing which fixture call produces the second finding and will adjust the structured field-count logic rather than weakening the policy assertion.

The implementation now covers the requested RHS distinctions, and the new policy fixtures include the two-field/two-argument surplus near miss. The shared build queue is saturated by other lanes; formatting and diff checks are clean while the policy rerun waits for a slot.

All three policy-fixture tests now pass, including all eight issue rows and the incomplete-shape cases. The mismatch came from treating an unused positional argument on a named-only format as surplus; I changed that missing-name fixture to `.format()` so it isolates the missing named argument, while retaining the campaign’s two-field surplus near miss. I’m moving on to clippy and the vocabulary registry tests.

The helper change is staged for validation; the earlier clippy report is only from the pre-fix eight-argument version. Shared clippy and formatting jobs from parallel lanes are competing for the build queue, so both checks are still running.

Clippy also caught an exhaustive match in the semantic test suite that needs an arm for the new RQL step. I’m adding the appropriate fixture application there; this is a compile error caused by the new public query variant, so I’ll include it in the post-merge gate.

The read-ledger test now exercises the new step on an actual Python `.format()` call, rather than merely adding a match arm to the existing TypeScript fixture. The clippy rerun and final formatting check are queued; the earlier compile findings are being addressed in the same gate.

The latest clippy pass has moved past the earlier helper lint and is checking the root test targets after the ledger-case addition. Formatting and whitespace checks are clean; once this run settles, I’ll rerun the three policy checks on the final helper shape and proceed to the required merge train gate.

The merged tree passes `cargo fmt --all --check`, and the merge itself introduced no unresolved version or epoch change for this query-time work. The post-merge clippy and combined regression/registry test commands are waiting behind other lanes in the shared cargo-slot queue.

I spotted one scope mismatch before the queued post-merge suite started: boolean literals were being treated as definite non-mappings, though the parent’s accepted set names list, tuple, set, string, and numeric literals. I stopped the still-queued test command, narrowed booleans to typed-incomplete, and added a fixture so the post-merge gate checks the exact approved boundary.

The final RHS boundary is now encoded: boolean literals produce typed-incomplete rows, while the approved list/tuple/set/string/numeric cases stay definite. The combined post-merge test run and clippy are queued/running against that committed correction; formatting is clean.

On the py07-combined branch, all 59 Python tests and the PythonRuleFact relation test pass; the declaration-kind registry remains the same master-only producer gap. The final strict clippy run has started against the merged exception and format code.
